title: Curriculum Leadership Checklists
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart offers a set of checklists for senior and subject leaders who must deliver a high quality curriculum at scale through many colleagues. He starts with the subject overview, a single document showing the whole sequence of units so leaders can check national curriculum coverage, quality assure sequencing and explain every deliberate content choice, and he warns against separate overviews per year group, which erode coherence across key stages. He criticises the habit of letting six-week half terms dictate how many units are taught, arguing that unit length should follow what is worth learning. Next come key concepts that thread through the age range and anchor both pupil schemata and teacher subject-knowledge CPD, then a unit structure that works backwards from a disciplinarily valid composite task through smaller components instead of lessons. He closes with the idea of subject-specific active ingredients, such as those in Ofsted's history research review, as the basis for CPD, and ends with a consolidated thirteen-point checklist.
points: Keep one whole-sequence overview per subject so coverage, sequencing and the reasons behind each content choice are visible at a glance.
Decide unit length by what is valuable to learn rather than by the six-week half-term pattern, which produces a cramped and rushed curriculum.
Name the key concepts that run through the age range and build teacher subject-knowledge CPD around them.
Design units backwards from a composite task that is valid for the discipline, and think in components rather than lessons because the lesson is the wrong unit of time.
Define each subject's active ingredients (its characteristic pedagogies) and base CPD on expertise in them.
quotes: Whether a senior leader in charge of the curriculum or a subject leader in charge of one or a number of individual subjects, the challenge is the same. A high quality education provided at scale by multiple colleagues.
A mistake is to have several overviews, perhaps one per year group. If each year group is free to make their own curricular choices, the risk is a lack of coherence within and across key stages.
Far better to decide what is valuable to learn and let that decide the length of units of work rather than being defined by the six week pattern of half terms.
Building subject knowledge of key concepts is useful way of doing this because of how important those concepts are in developing children’s understanding of the subject over time.
An important consideration here is that the composite task is disciplinarily valid. Writing a newspaper report about the Romans is not history.
Note that these are not referred to as lessons, but as components. That’s because the lesson is the wrong unit of time.
Many subjects will have specific pedagogies relevant to teaching that content and it is well worth considering these as part of a subject strategy that informs CPD.
